nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What are microplastics (MPs) and how are they produced?
nodes.answer: Microplastics (MPs) are tiny particles of plastic that are produced mainly through human activities such as shipping, fishing, and aquaculture, and can also be added indirectly to mangroves via rivers, surface runoff, and sewage systems.
nodes.paragraph: Plastic pollution: a threat to mangrove ecosystems Plastic production has experienced a great increase since the 1940s, which aligns with its widespread utilization in various sectors such as industry, agriculture, and health- care (Mehmood et al. 2023). Regardless, multiple uses of plastic in the form of waste carry substantial ecological repercussions. Long-term persistence of plastic waste under - goes weathering and breakdown into tiny particles such as microplastics (< 5 mm) and nanoplastics (NPs) (< 100 nm) (Mehmood et al. 2022). MPs are mostly released directly by human activities like shipping, fishing, and aquaculture. MPs are also added indi- rectly to mangroves by rivers, surface runoff, and sewage systems (Mehmood et al. 2023). MPs have been detected in remote coastal areas, marine water, deep-sea sediments, and glaciers and have also been found in numerous marine species (Mehmood and Peng 2022). These small particles will remain in the environment for a long time before they decompose, enter the food chain, or settle down in sedi- ments.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: Within what depth range do the majority of microplastics accumulate in surface sediments?
nodes.answer: The majority of microplastics tend to accumulate in surface sediments, especially within the upper 5 cm.
nodes.paragraph: Due to their lower density than seawater, these par - ticles tend to float on the water before eventually settling on the seabed or accumulating in sediments in mangrove eco- systems (Mehmood and Peng 2022, Mehmood et al. 2023). The majority of MPs tend to accumulate in surface sedi- ments, especially within the upper 5 cm, mostly due to alter - ations in density and/or biotransformation (Riaz et al. 2024, Vidayanti and Retnaningdyah 2024). Several factors, includ- ing (1) biological feeding, (2) agglomeration, (3) hydroe- lectric disturbance, and (4) adsorption of larger particles, directly influence the settling of MPs (Alomar et al. 2016; Bao et al. 2022 ). Previous studies have ascribed sediment as one of the key reservoirs for MP accumulation in the marine environment (Barrett et al. 2020; Lin et al. 2024). Barrett et al. (2020) reported massive MPs (14 million tons) in sea sediments worldwide. Various factors, including shipping, fishing, and aquaculture, directly release MPs into coastal areas.

nodes.question: What are some factors that influence the settling of microplastics?
nodes.answer: Factors affecting the settling of microplastics include biological feeding, agglomeration, hydroelectric disturbance, and adsorption of larger particles.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What are some ways that microplastics (MPs) are transported to mangrove ecosystems?
nodes.answer: Microplastics are transported to mangrove ecosystems through rivers, surface runoff, sewage systems, and wind-driven deposition from beaches and waste disposal sites.
nodes.paragraph: Rivers, surface runoff, and sewage systems indirectly transport MPs, influencing mangrove ecosystems (Mehmood et al. 2023). Wind-driven deposition on beaches and proxim- ity to waste disposal sites also play a significant role in the deposition of MPs in coastal areas (Riaz et al. 2024). Mangrove ecosystems have been found to have substan- tially higher MP contamination as compared to other eco - systems (Liu et al. 2022). Plastic presence in mangrove eco- systems constitutes a significant portion of overall marine debris, as evidenced by recent studies (Browne et al. 2007; Li et al. 2021). Regardless, most studies focus on plastic waste (Browne et al. 2007), while studies on MPs in man- groves are still in their infancy. Previous research found that the mangrove sediment had a higher concentration of MPs compared to the marine sediment in the Beibu Gulf, China. That means the difference was substantially high: 264 2 items/kg in mangrove sediment compared to 0 11 1 items/ kg in marine sediments (Jiao et al. 2021).

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What are microplastics (MPs) mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Microplastics (MPs) are harmful substances that contribute to environmental pollution and compromise the sustainability of mangrove ecosystems.
nodes.paragraph: 2021). Untreated sewage hinders the propagation of mangroves and can contribute to the acid- ification of local waters (Saher et al. 2019). The release of untreated waste into the ocean directly leads to an increase in ocean acidification (Weis 2024). As the largest city in Pakistan with a population of over 20 million, poor waste management practices have unfortunately turned Karachi S seashores into dumping grounds (Afzal et al. 2024). The absence of treatment plants for harmful substances, includ- ing microplastics (MPs), continuously resales the environ- ment, compromising mangrove ecosystem sustainability (Riaz et al. 2024). This work provides insight into the functions of man- groves in CO2 management and potential risks associated with water pollutants, particularly MPs. We also discussed the sources of MPs and their environmental and ecological implications for coastal and mangrove ecosystems. In sum- mary, this study highlights the need for effective research and the establishment of improved plastic waste manage- ment practices to reduce the release and introduction of MPs in mangrove ecosystems, especially in Pakistan. The manu- script emphasizes further research on behavior, accumula- tion, and the impact of MPs in these coastal and mangrove environments.

nodes.label: Science and Tech
nodes.question: How do the structures of polyethylene-degrading proteins from wax worm saliva help in plastic degradation?
nodes.answer: The near-atomic resolution structures of the hexamerism in wax worm saliva provide insights into the mechanism by which these proteins degrade polyethylene, offering potential solutions for plastic waste management.
